1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Two-stage least squares (IV).
- Logic: We want the causal effect of the average education of one’s state-of-birth cohort (aggregate human capital) on individual wages, holding own education constant. Average education is endogenous (selection, sorting, agglomeration). Compulsory schooling and child labor laws shifted schooling for specific state-of-birth × birth-year cohorts. Use those law-driven shocks as instruments for cohort average education. Include own education as a control to net out private returns; the IV coefficient recovers the externality (social) effect provided the laws affect wages only through education.
- Complementary diagnostics: Reduced-form/event-study plots of wages and schooling vs. distance-to-reform within birth state to assess pre-trends and instrument relevance.

2. Treatment and Control
- Endogenous treatment variable: Average years of schooling for men age 40–49 in the same state-of-birth × birth-year (equivalently, state-of-birth × Census-year) cell as the individual. Use leave-one-out means at the individual level to avoid mechanical correlation with own schooling.
- Instruments (Z, at state-of-birth × birth-year level):
  1) Compulsory attendance age exposure applicable during school ages for that cohort.
  2) Child labor law strength/exposure applicable during school ages for that cohort.
  These generate exogenous shifts in schooling at the cohort-by-state level.
- Control group/counterfactual: Cohorts and states where laws were less binding or changed later serve as comparison; identification comes from differential timing and intensity of law changes across states and cohorts.
- Timing: The “event” is the cohort’s exposure to a stricter law around school ages (typically ages 14–17). Outcomes measured decades later when individuals are 40–49 in 1960/70/80 Censuses.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Relevance: Compulsory schooling and child labor laws increased schooling for affected cohorts in their state of birth. Empirically well-established; we will verify a strong first stage.
- Exclusion (conditional on own education): Conditional on individual’s own years of schooling and fixed effects, the laws affect wages at ages 40–49 only through the education of the cohort (average education) and own education. This rules out direct long-run law effects on wages unrelated to education (we mitigate with rich fixed effects and migration controls).
- Independence: Conditional on state-of-birth FE, birth-year FE, census-year FE, and destination state × census-year FE, the timing of a state’s school law changes is as good as random with respect to unobserved shocks to wages of birth cohorts.
- Monotonicity: Tightening compulsory schooling/child labor laws did not reduce schooling for any compliers in the affected cohorts (no defiers).
- Stable composition/measurement: Group averages computed from large PUMS cells reliably measure cohort schooling; leave-one-out means prevent mechanical own-mean correlation.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Selective migration and destination wage differences:
  - Threat: Law-induced increases in schooling may raise migration to high-wage destinations; wage gains could reflect moving to productive places rather than spillovers from peers.
  - Mitigation: Define exposure and instrument by state of birth (pre-determined). Include destination state × census-year fixed effects so comparisons are within the same labor market and year among workers born in different states. The IV coefficient then uses only across–state-of-birth, across-cohort variation, holding destination-year conditions fixed.
- Direct policy confounding and cohort trends:
  - Threat: States that reformed early also adopted other cohort-targeted policies (e.g., school quality investments) that raise wages independent of years of schooling.
  - Mitigation: Include state-of-birth FE, birth-year FE, census-year FE; add region-by-birth-year FE or state-of-birth × birth-decade FE as robustness; use multiple instruments (compulsory attendance and child labor laws) and overidentification tests; where possible, control for baseline state-of-birth characteristics interacted with cohort (e.g., manufacturing share at age 14).
- Measurement and mechanical correlation:
  - Threat: Average education is measured with sampling error and mechanically correlates with own education.
  - Mitigation: Use leave-one-out cell means; instrument the cell mean with laws; weight by cell size; report weak-IV-robust confidence intervals and first-stage F-statistics.

5. R Code Outline
Notes:
- Replace file paths and variable names to match your data. Assumes IPUMS has variables: year, age, sex, wage_wk, educ_yrs, state_birth, state_res, race, perwt.
- Laws file assumed to have: state_birth, yob (birth year), c_attend_exp (compulsory attendance exposure), clabor_exp (child labor exposure).

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(sandwich)
library(clubSandwich) # for CR2 SEs if desired

# 1) Load data
ipums <- fread("ipums_males_40to49.csv")
laws  <- fread("laws_by_statebirth_yob.csv")

# 2) Sample restrictions and core variables
# Keep men 40-49 with valid wages and schooling
dt <- ipums[sex == "male" & age >= 40 & age <= 49]
# Keep employed with positive weekly wages
dt <- dt[!is.na(wage_wk) & wage_wk > 0 & !is.na(educ_yrs)]
# Log wages
dt[, ln_wage := log(wage_wk)]
# Ensure coding as factors where appropriate
dt[, `:=`(
  state_birth = as.factor(state_birth),
  state_res   = as.factor(state_res),
  race        = as.factor(race),
  year        = as.integer(year),
  yob         = as.integer(yob) # year of birth
)]
# Weights
if (!"perwt" %in% names(dt)) dt[, perwt := 1]

# 3) Merge laws by state of birth × birth year
laws[, `:=`(
  state_birth = as.factor(state_birth),
  yob = as.integer(yob)
)]
dt <- merge(dt, laws, by = c("state_birth", "yob"), all.x = TRUE)

# 4) Construct group (state of birth × birth year) and destination-year FE id
dt[, g_sb_yob := interaction(state_birth, yob, drop = TRUE)]
dt[, dest_year := interaction(state_res, year, drop = TRUE)]

# 5) Construct leave-one-out average education at g = (state_birth × yob)
# Weighted by person weights
dt[, sum_edu := sum(educ_yrs * perwt, na.rm = TRUE), by = g_sb_yob]
dt[, n_wt    := sum(perwt, na.rm = TRUE),               by = g_sb_yob]
# Leave-one-out numerator and denom
dt[, loo_num := sum_edu - educ_yrs * perwt, by = g_sb_yob]
dt[, loo_den := n_wt - perwt,                by = g_sb_yob]
dt[, avg_edu_loo := fifelse(loo_den > 0, loo_num / loo_den, NA_real_)]

# 6) Define instruments (can use both for over-ID)
# Center/scale optional for numerics
dt[, z_attend := c_attend_exp]
dt[, z_clabor := clabor_exp]

# 7) Fixed effects and controls
# Birth-year FE and state-of-birth FE are added via fixest FE
# Age fixed effects:
dt[, age_f := as.factor(age)]
# Optional: birth-decade for robustness trends
dt[, birth_dec := as.factor(10L * (yob %/% 10L))]

# 8) Main 2SLS: ln_wage on avg_edu_loo (endog), instrumented by laws; control for own educ and rich FE
# FE: state_of_birth, birth_year, census year, destination state × year
# Cluster SEs at instrument variation level: state_birth × yob (g_sb_yob)
main_iv <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ educ_yrs + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year | 
    avg_edu_loo ~ z_attend + z_clabor,
  data = dt, weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob
)
summary(main_iv, stage = 1)  # first stage
summary(main_iv, stage = 2)  # second stage

# Report Kleibergen-Paap rk F-stat (weak IV robust)
fitstat(main_iv, type = "ivf")

# 9) Reduced form and first stage checks (optional)
# First stage: avg_edu_loo on instruments and FE
fs <- feols(avg_edu_loo ~ z_attend + z_clabor + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year,
            data = dt, weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob)
summary(fs)

# Reduced form: ln_wage on instruments with own education as control
rf <- feols(ln_wage ~ z_attend + z_clabor + educ_yrs + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year,
            data = dt, weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob)
summary(rf)

# 10) Robustness A: use only one instrument at a time
iv_attend <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ educ_yrs + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year |
    avg_edu_loo ~ z_attend,
  data = dt, weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob
)
summary(iv_attend, stage = 2)

iv_clabor <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ educ_yrs + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year |
    avg_edu_loo ~ z_clabor,
  data = dt, weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob
)
summary(iv_clabor, stage = 2)

# 11) Robustness B: add state-of-birth × birth-decade FE (state-specific cohort trends)
dt[, sob_dec := interaction(state_birth, birth_dec, drop = TRUE)]
iv_trend <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ educ_yrs + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year + sob_dec |
    avg_edu_loo ~ z_attend + z_clabor,
  data = dt, weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob
)
summary(iv_trend, stage = 2)

# 12) Optional: leave-out-at-cell-level check (drop cells with very small n)
cell_n <- unique(dt[, .(g_sb_yob, n_wt)])
small_cells <- cell_n[n_wt < 50, g_sb_yob]
iv_n50 <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ educ_yrs + age_f + race | state_birth + yob + year + dest_year |
    avg_edu_loo ~ z_attend + z_clabor,
  data = dt[!g_sb_yob %in% small_cells], weights = ~ perwt, cluster = ~ g_sb_yob
)
summary(iv_n50, stage = 2)
```

Interpretation: The coefficient on avg_edu_loo in the 2SLS is the spillover (externality) elasticity of wages with respect to peers’ average years of schooling (holding own schooling fixed). Multiply by 100 for percent change in wages per additional year of average schooling.

6. Expected Results
- Direction: Positive social returns. Being in a more educated state-of-birth cohort should raise wages, beyond own schooling, via knowledge spillovers, adoption of better technologies, and agglomeration.
- Magnitude: A plausible prior is 1–2% higher wages per additional average year of schooling of the cohort (holding own education constant), consistent with moderate externalities found in related work.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
- C1: Strong first stage (laws shift schooling meaningfully): 1
- C2: Exclusion restriction (laws affect wages only via education; we condition on own education and include rich FE): 0.5 (plausible but potentially threatened by correlated cohort-targeted policies and school quality)
- C3: Independence from migration/destination shocks (controlled by destination × year FE): 1
- C4: Monotonicity (no defiers; laws don’t reduce schooling): 1
- C5: Measurement/composition validity for group averages (leave-one-out means; drop small cells; weight by cell size): 1

Notes and extensions
- Event-study diagnostic: Plot reduced-form outcomes (avg schooling and wages) by cohort relative to reform year within state of birth to visualize pre-trends.
- Alternative outcomes: Employment, hours, and wage residuals (e.g., conditioning on occupation) to test channels.
- Overidentification: If both instruments are used, report Hansen J-test and compare point estimates across single-instrument specifications.
